root.text:
Hey folks, Eric invited me here. I'm the program lead at <https://summerofbitcoin.org/|Summer of Bitcoin>, a non-profit that runs a global internship program for university students to work on bitcoin FOSS.

If you'd like to sign up and get a couple of interns work on your favorite project ideas under your mentorship, here's all the info you need:

*Quick recap on how the program works:*
1. Bitcoin open-source devs / designers sign up as mentors.
2. Mentors provide project ideas from their respective projects.
3. University students apply, get screened and submit a project proposal using the project idea as a starting point.
4. Mentors evaluate and select project proposals.
5. Students contribute code / design during the project period, as outlined in their proposals.
6. Mentors guide their mentees wherever they're stuck and help with reviews.

*On time commitment from mentors:* 
We have typically seen mentors do a 30-60 min call once per week to discuss progress and unblock their interns on critical issues. Most teams simply add the intern to their weekly stand-up and work with them just like any other member of the team. Some also go totally async in their comms, especially when the project is relatively straightforward and the candidate is self-driven. We leave this part completely on both the mentor and their intern to figure out.

*Timeline:*
1. Application period: Feb 1 - Feb 15.
2. Bootcamp: Feb 16 - Mar 31.
3. Proposal period: Apr 1 - Apr 30.
4. Results announced: May 7.
5. Project period: May 15 to Aug 15.

*What does a project idea look like?*
Project ideas are scoped for a university-level student with a basic background in CS / UX design and bitcoin fundamentals. Project should be achievable over 12-weeks. Template for a project idea is available here: <https://docs.google.com/document/d/1wQV5rhZ5DC5HO89K5-AVWkZLK3-QhqVPjjPQDwHzSZc/edit>

Some project ideas from prior years for reference:
• SOB-miniscript-bip322: <https://docs.google.com/document/d/1gY45fEMMl6QGObUbGHM4Ehzp1GLQq060TsOQOM0wteY/edit?usp=sharing>
• SOB-Electrs-Benchmarking: <https://docs.google.com/document/d/1sPScosbJNKIHCa5wSjZ8sc5cPNqAHXoJMGqHKoVCDUo/edit?usp=sharing>
• SOB-LDK-lnprototest: <https://docs.google.com/document/d/1aNOSNMYGeaeh-NL2DmGEodJ_le754kILJ35rUuGA3kY/edit?usp=sharing>
• SOB-LN-Research-PriceOfAnarchy: <https://docs.google.com/document/d/1zm5n-O0bSEbXmDN49oLFAa0YuVzFABwndJwFRO73I6g/edit?usp=sharing>
*When do we need project ideas from you?*
We're looking to publish project ideas on our website by the _end of this month_, which is quite close already. But feel free to take a couple of additional days if you need. You can submit as many project ideas as you want. Here's a form to submit them: <https://www.jotform.com/form/240533114662044>.

As a token of gratitude, mentors receive a gift of $500 in BTC once the program successfully concludes :slightly_smiling_face:

Let me know if you have any further questions!

We didn't hold the weekly today, so here's a quick update on my end. I was in London for a few days, home for a day, and then in FL for a few days. Managed to get some work done though.

As you saw above, I was working out the algorithm to accurately detect malleability, which I haven't found anywhere. Core doesn't have it right and then interleave it with Merkle tree computation. Despite this complexity it's far less efficient. Their algorithm is:
It's confusing but if
*mutated
starts true then it attempts to set
mutation
and then returns that back in the
*mutated

in/out parameter. As you can see, for each row of Merkle computation it compares all hashes in the row as pairs - even though only the last pair can cause mutation. And that only happens on odd count rows - as a result of the
push_back(hashes.back())
statement. And that can only result when the
log2(count)
of the duplicated hashes equals the depth of the first odd row. So clearly there is a lot of extra iteration and comparison happening.
I've implemented, tested and merged several functions on
system::chain::block
to use in node and database. The core algorithm is this:

Given an integer count of tx hashes (set) and a proposed size of the duplicated hashes (width) the algorithm returns true if the set is mutable for the width. By enumerating all widths up to half the set size one determines all possible mutations. The sets of trailing txs that may make up a mutation can then be compared for duplication. On average that's an average of 1 comparison per block - at least for up to 44 txs (well below O(log(n))). By comparison Core's test is O(n) for any block.

Lost a day tracking a confirmation check failure.

In the node confirmation checks are implemented in store queries. The general purpose system::chain object checks (header/block/tx) are retained, but those expect fully populated objects and metadata fully populated from the store. These are used in header/tx/block check/accept/connect, but the last stage (confirm) is not implemented with the expectation of deserialized objects, and is distinct from validation due to the concurrency differences (validation is concurrent while confirmation is sequential - spentness implies ordering).

So to track down the failure I implemented a redundant confirmation test against the failing transaction - one with the chain objects and the other by query. The chain object test succeeded and comparison showed that the check
tx.version >= relative_locktime_min_version
was missing.

Spent some time working out the query to handle the three forks that make up bip30 handling. This is the only one I hadn't worked out in the design, because it wasn't absolutely necessary. But for consistency we should have it as in some fork configurations it must be applied. It can be costly to implement, but I worked out a constant time solution.

The difficulty for us arises from parallel writes with minimal locking. It is possible to end up with duplicate instances of
any

block, header, tx... in the store. This is the result of races, but extremely rare and logically a non-issue. But in this one case, the number of instances of a duplicated coinbase tx matter, and the instances of associated confirmations of it, spends of it, and confirmations of the spenders. So it presented a bit of a challenge.

But I found that, because every spend association commits to is spending tx by surrogate key, and every tx confirmation commits to its confirming block, we can count up the total number of uniquely confirmed (by block key) duplicated coinbases, and the total number of unique spends (by spender key) uniquely confirmed. The difference gives us the desired result - 0 means all spent, 1 means one unspent, -n and n> means fault, n > 1 means fault. Since each query iterates only these unique instances and they are essentially always singletons, it's not too costly if/when it's enabled.

Just implemented the `bip30` check, which turned out a bit simpler than I described previously. More interestingly, it is almost free in the no-duplicates case, and a trivial cost in the duplicates case (which don't actually exist). This is considered a really expensive check by Core:

"The BIP30 check is expensive, as it requires going through all the outputs of all the transactions in the block, and checking if a UTxO with the same outpoint does not already exist."

Or just a single constant time hashmap lookup. :joy:

<https://bitcoin.stackexchange.com/a/120839/34482>

elements.text: Our custom hashmap allows iteration over duplicates. Any hash table must implement conflict lists for a given hash bucket. Our average list length is configured for ~1.5 conflicts. If a duplicate entry is created it naturally hides older entries (this is how we implement logical delete for reorg and progressive state changes during validation). However our primitives allow enumeration of the conflict list, so that any hash table can also be treated as a multimap. A simple iterator hides (steps over) non-matching conflicts, making the enumeration seamless.

This is an example of Core pushing forks to try and mitigate performance issues that are a consequence of their implementation, not inherent to consensus. bip30 defined a soft fork, which was necessary. And of course there is an ongoing effort to resolve it again now that it becomes reenabled at that future point.

elements.text: Finally, I think I have a resolution to the open design flaw of hard termination on disk full. It's a hard problem since each table is expended independently and generally in the midst of a logical transaction. There is no transactional rollback, so there must be sufficient space. But by ensuring a minimal amount of disk space after expansion we can ensure that a subsequent expansion will succeed at least to the extent of committing the current transaction. Otherwise the process can be terminated safely. The only failure scenarios then is that the disk becomes filled external to the process (which we could also try to manage). But with snapshots this is pretty reaonable.

It's a hard problem since each table is expended independently and generally in the midst of a logical transaction. There is no transactional rollback, so there must be sufficient space. But by ensuring a minimal amount of disk space after expansion we can ensure that a subsequent expansion will succeed at least to the extent of committing the current transaction. Otherwise the process can be terminated safely. The only failure scenarios then is that the disk becomes filled external to the process (which we could also try to manage). But with snapshots this is pretty reaonable.

elements.text: With that done I've moved on to incorporating generation of the neutrino filters table. It looks like the initial design for this table isn't good. The compact headers need to be computed sequentially, and the filters need to be computed off of a deserialized block with populated prevouts (at least the
output.value

While validation is ordered, blocks are not confirmed until the subsequent confirmation step, which doesn't have access to a populated block. And since the filters are blobs and need to be linked from a header there is also a late association problem. Solvable, but not in the existing table design.
